title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM generation shared across arms), producing model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered maximum_model_calls for independent per‑arm generation = 400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this run. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial injection fraction, and model‑call budgeting) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the supplied bundle (execution/*, analysis/*) and permit deterministic replay.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operator productivity gains for network operations (NetOps) but raises operational safety risks: an incorrect or ill‑timed change can break reachability, violate policy, or cause outages. Recent work therefore proposes tool‑grounding, deterministic validators, and generate–validate–repair architectures to improve correctness and reduce hallucination‑driven errors. Motivated by these proposals and calls for workflow‑centred evaluation, we preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) to measure whether deterministic verifier augmentation reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe configuration proposals from a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial prompts.

Our preregistered research question was: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic validator → optional repair) change the rate of unsafe network‑change proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts? To answer this with controlled causal inference we specified a paired binary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (SAFE encoded as 1). The paired design, sample size (N=200 tasks), test, and handling of technical failures were frozen before execution and are archived in the preregistration manifest. The contribution of this paper is methodological: (1) we publish a complete, archived confirmatory run with full deterministic artifacts; (2) we present an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the confirmatory test produced no discordant pairs (a ceiling/testability failure caused by shared generation semantics combined with a zero baseline unsafe rate); and (3) we provide concrete, reproducible recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial injection budgeting, and model‑call accounting) to make future repeats informative.
sections.related_work: Surveys and prototype reports document the rapid emergence of LLM applications in NetOps (intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis, and limited remediation) and recommend verifier‑in‑the‑loop architectures and workflow‑centred evaluations. Representative items in our verified literature collection include recent survey/prototype analyses and methodological critiques that motivate deterministic sandboxing, generate–validate–repair pipelines, and red‑teaming to measure guardrail efficacy. Prior experimental work shows task‑dependent gains from tool‑augmentation and self‑verification, but effect sizes depend strongly on verifier fidelity, prompt design, and generation semantics. Complementary guardrail and red‑teaming literature emphasizes safety/utility trade‑offs (false refusals versus undetected unsafe proposals) and prescribes replayable, sandboxed evaluations with archived traces and deterministic validators; these methodological prescriptions directly informed our preregistered design and choice of deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Our paper does not claim novel verifier algorithms; instead it contributes a fully archived, preregistered empirical run and analysis that expose evaluation design pitfalls relevant to the community.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered as cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1. The primary estimand was the paired difference in SAFE rates (guarded minus baseline). The paired binary design with N=200 paired tasks and exact McNemar two‑sided testing was specified in the preregistration. The analysis executor and CI method (paired bootstrap, 10000 resamples, seed = 1729) were frozen prior to data collection. All preregistered elements (task generator, adversarial template rules, failure handling, and stopping rules) are archived.

Task generator, adversarial templates, and sampling plan. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks under a preregistered RNG schedule (seed=42; task seeds 1..200). Tasks targeted operationally meaningful changes limited to admin, mtu, and vlan fields across single‑AS, multi‑device topologies. The sampling plan grouped tasks into benign and adversarial clusters; adversarial prompts were generated by templated obfuscation, negation/implication transforms, and privilege‑escalation phrasing described in the preregistration. The full task manifest is archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl and representative payloads are included under execution/representative_tasks in the artifact bundle.

Pipelines, generation semantics, and model‑call budgeting. Two pipelines were compared: (a) baseline LLM‑only, and (b) guarded pipeline that passes the LLM candidate through deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and supports a single automatic repair attempt. The preregistration permitted two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation (each arm receives an independent LLM call) or shared_initial_candidate (one LLM generation shared across arms). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing one LLM generation per task shared by both arms. This choice reduced model_calls_used to 200; the preregistered independent per‑arm plan would have required up to 400 model calls for N=200. Model identity and configuration are recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = "gpt‑5‑mini", max_output_tokens = 1500). The execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) records completed_episode_count = 400, model_calls_used = 200, and failed_episode_count = 0.

Deterministic validator and scoring. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in a sandbox and implemented full_intent_constraint_validation rules to label proposals as SAFE/UNSAFE and to produce detailed validation_before/after traces. For confirmatory episodes no automatic repairs were applied (repair_provider_trace = null in scoring JSONs). Scoring files (execution/scoring/*.json) contain normalized_configuration, parsed command counts, validator verdicts, violation lists, and structured difficulty metadata; these artifacts are the basis for the binary outcomes used by the analysis executor.

Analysis executor and handling of missingness. paired_binary_analysis_v1 assembled the paired contingency table and computed an exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value and the paired bootstrap percentile CI. Missingness rules (one automatic retry per failed model call, exclusions/replacements for contamination flags, abort thresholds at >10% technical failures) were preregistered and implemented in the execution harness. The run produced zero technical failures and no exclusions; analysis/missingness_summary.csv records these counts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and raw outcomes. The run completed planned_episode_count = 400 with failed_episode_count = 0 and model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task). The preregistered independent per‑arm generation budget would have allocated maximum_model_calls = 400 for the paired design; this difference is recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json.

Condition summary and paired contingency table. analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline SAFE successes = 200/200 and guarded SAFE successes = 200/200 (SAFE encoded as 1), producing observed SAFE rates of 1.0 for both arms. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) shows n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). These numeric results are present in analysis/results.json and the CSV artifacts.

Representative scoring traces. Representative per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and task-000001-guarded.json, among others) show identical shared_initial_candidate content and validator traces reporting violation_count = 0 and valid = true in validation_before and validation_after blocks. The deterministic_reconciliation artifact (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) confirms consistent episode accounting (complete_pair_count = 200, hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, all deterministic checks passed). No repairs were exercised: repair_provider_trace fields are null across sampled confirmatory scoring files.

Diagnostic interpretation (artifact evidence). Three artifact‑grounded facts explain the non‑informative confirmatory outcome: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics caused identical LLM candidate strings for each pair (evidence: execution/responses/* and execution/provider_calls/*); (2) for the sampled tasks gpt‑5‑mini produced proposals that passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (evidence: execution/scoring/*.json with violation_count = 0); and (3) model_call budgeting limited calls to one per task rather than two, eliminating the per‑arm generation variance necessary to produce discordant pairs. All referenced artifacts are archived and enumerated in the execution and analysis directories.
sections.discussion:
Why the paired test was degenerate. McNemar's paired test gains power only from discordant pairs (n10, n01). Under shared_initial_candidate semantics, both arms received identical generation outputs; therefore the only possible discordance would arise if the guarded arm applied an automatic repair that changed SAFE→UNSAFE coding or vice versa. In our run no repairs were applied and the baseline proposals were all SAFE, yielding n10 = n01 = 0 and a degenerate contingency. The manifested consequence is a non‑informative confirmatory test rather than evidence about verifier efficacy.

Design recommendations for informative repeats (artifact‑grounded). Based on the preregistration and execution accounting we recommend the following concrete protocol changes to make a repeat informative: (1) use independent per‑arm generation by default for paired causal tests — for N=200 this requires ~200 additional LLM calls (change model_calls_used from 200 → 400); (2) preregister and calibrate an adversarial injection fraction so baseline unsafe rates are nonzero under the target model (for example, inject explicit unsafe templates for 10–20% of tasks to ensure nonzero discordant mass while preserving naturalistic coverage); (3) reserve exploratory samples (the preregistration allowed up to 50 exploratory tasks) to estimate verifier ROC (true positive and false positive rates) before confirmatory testing; (4) if budget constrained, consider alternative estimands (absolute unsafe rates with independent repeated draws in a single arm) rather than a paired McNemar test. Each recommendation maps to a concrete artifact or budget figure present in the preregistration and execution manifest.

Operational implications and cautious messaging. This run should not be read as empirical evidence that verifiers are unnecessary or universally ineffective; rather it is a reproducible methodological artifact demonstrating how generation semantics and budgeting choices can make a preregistered causal test untestable. Practitioners designing verifier evaluations should ensure that generation semantics permit the causal contrast of interest and that the model‑call budget supports independent draws where required. The archived artifacts provide exact accounting that supports these operational prescriptions.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated in this run. The scientific contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑oriented: (1) we publish a complete preregistered run with deterministic artifacts enabling exact replay; (2) we provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) we provide concrete, archived recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial budgeting, model‑call accounting) to design informative repeats. The archived execution and analysis bundle (execution/* and analysis/*) permits deterministic replays and community replication.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
